title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: It had been a long time since Rostov had enjoyed music as much as he did that day. But the moment Natasha finished her barcarolle, reality came crashing back. He got up without a word and went downstairs to his own room. Fifteen minutes later the old count came home from his club, cheerful and pleased with himself. Nicholas, hearing the carriage pull up, went to meet him.
"Well — did you have a good time?" said the old count, beaming proudly at his son.
Nicholas tried to say "Yes," but could barely get the word out — he nearly burst into sobs. The count was lighting his pipe and didn't notice his son's state.

"It can't be helped!" thought Nicholas, for the first and last time. And suddenly, in the most casual tone he could manage — a tone that made him ashamed of himself — he said, as if merely asking his father for the carriage to go into town:
"Papa, I've come about a matter of business. I nearly forgot. I need some money."
"Oh dear!" said his father, who was in an especially good mood. "I told you it wouldn't be enough. How much?"

"Quite a lot," said Nicholas, flushing, and with a stupid, careless smile for which he could never forgive himself afterward. "I've lost a little — I mean a good deal, a great deal — forty-three thousand."
"What! To whom? Nonsense!" cried the count, suddenly reddening with a rush of blood to his neck and the back of his head, the way old men do.
"I promised to pay tomorrow," said Nicholas.
"Well!" said the old count, spreading out his arms and sinking helplessly onto the sofa.

"It can't be helped! It happens to everyone!" said the son in a bold, offhand tone, while deep in his soul he saw himself as a worthless scoundrel whose entire life couldn't make up for his crime. He longed to kiss his father's hands and beg forgiveness on his knees, yet he spoke in a careless, even rude voice, saying that it happens to everyone!
The old count dropped his eyes at his son's words and began frantically searching around for something.
"Yes, yes," he muttered, "it'll be hard, I'm afraid — hard to raise... happens to everybody! Yes, who hasn't done it?"
And with a furtive glance at his son's face, the count left the room. Nicholas had been prepared for resistance, but had not at all expected this.
"Papa! Papa!" he called after him, sobbing. "Forgive me!" And seizing his father's hand, he pressed it to his lips and burst into tears.
While father and son were having this conversation, the mother and daughter were having one no less important. Natasha came running to her mother, breathless with excitement.
"Mama! Mama! He's made me..."
"Made what?"
"Made me — he's proposed, Mama! Mama!" she exclaimed.
The countess couldn't believe her ears. Denisov had proposed. To whom? To this slip of a girl, Natasha, who not long ago was playing with dolls and was still having lessons.
"Don't be silly, Natasha! What nonsense!" she said, hoping it was a joke.
"Nonsense indeed! I'm telling you it's true," said Natasha indignantly. "I've come to ask you what to do, and you call it 'nonsense!'"
The countess shrugged her shoulders.
"If it's true that Monsieur Denisov has proposed to you, tell him he's a fool — that's all!"
"No, he's not a fool!" replied Natasha, indignant and serious.
"Well then, what do you want? You're all in love these days. Fine — if you're in love, marry him!" said the countess with an annoyed laugh. "Good luck to you!"
"No, Mama, I'm not in love with him. I don't think I'm in love with him."
"Well then, tell him so."
"Mama, are you angry? Don't be angry, darling! Is it my fault?"
"No, but what is all this, my dear? Do you want me to go tell him?" said the countess with a smile.

"No, I'll do it myself — just tell me what to say. It's easy for you," said Natasha, smiling back. "You should have seen how he said it! I know he didn't mean to say it — it just slipped out accidentally."
"Well, all the same, you must refuse him."
"No, I can't. I feel so sorry for him! He's so nice."
"Well then, accept his proposal. It's high time you were married," the countess answered sharply and sarcastically.
"No, Mama, but I feel so sorry for him. I don't know how to say it."
"And there's nothing for you to say. I'll speak to him myself," said the countess, indignant that anyone should dare treat this little Natasha as a grown-up.

"No, absolutely not! I'll tell him myself, and you can listen at the door," and Natasha ran through the drawing room to the ballroom, where Denisov sat on the same chair by the clavichord with his face in his hands.
He jumped up at the sound of her light step.
"Nataly," he said, rushing toward her with quick steps, "decide my fate. It is in your hands."
"Vasili Dmitrich, I feel so sorry for you! No, but you are so nice... but it won't do... not that... but as a friend, I will always love you."

Denisov bent over her hand, and she heard strange sounds she didn't understand. She kissed his rough, curly black head. At that instant they heard the quick rustle of the countess's dress. She came up to them.

"Vasili Dmitrich, I thank you for the honor," she said in an embarrassed voice that sounded severe to Denisov, "but my daughter is so young, and I would have thought that, as my son's friend, you would have spoken to me first. In that case you would not have forced me to give this refusal."
"Countess..." said Denisov, with downcast eyes and a guilty expression. He tried to say more but faltered.
Natasha could not bear seeing him in such distress. She began to sob aloud.

"Countess, I was wrong," Denisov continued in an unsteady voice, "but believe me, I adore your daughter and all your family so much that I would give my life twice over..." He looked at the countess, and seeing her stern face said: "Well, goodbye, Countess," and kissing her hand, he strode out of the room without looking at Natasha.

The next day Rostov saw Denisov off. He didn't want to stay another day in Moscow. All of Denisov's Moscow friends gave him a farewell party at the gypsies', with the result that he had no memory of how he was put in the sleigh or of the first three stages of his journey.

After Denisov's departure, Rostov spent another two weeks in Moscow without leaving the house, waiting for the money his father couldn't raise right away, and he spent most of his time in the girls' room.

Sonya was more tender and devoted to him than ever. It was as if she wanted to show him that his losses were something noble that made her love him all the more, but Nicholas now considered himself unworthy of her.

He filled the girls' albums with verses and music, and having at last sent Dolokhov the full forty-three thousand rubles and received his receipt, he left at the end of November — without taking leave of any of his acquaintances — to rejoin his regiment, which was already in Poland.
